q: An object placed in the path of cathode rays casts a sharp shadow on the end of the discharge tube. This shows that cathode rays:
o: Are deflected by a magnetic field
x: A sharp shadow forms only if the rays travel in straight lines from the cathode. Their negative charge and mass are shown by other experiments (deflection by fields, turning a paddle wheel).

q: In discharge-tube experiments, cathode rays can turn a light paddle wheel placed in their path. Textbooks take this to show that cathode rays:
o: Consist of particles with mass, which carry momentum
x: Turning the wheel needs a push, i.e. momentum, so the rays were taken to be material particles with mass and velocity. Straight-line travel is shown by the shadow experiment, and the charge by deflection in fields.

q: In an oil-drop experiment, the charges on four drops were found to be 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. These results are consistent with a charge on one electron of:
x: Every charge must be a whole-number multiple of e: 3.2, 4.8, 8.0 and 6.4 are 2, 3, 5 and 4 times 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is the smallest measured value but 4.8 is not a whole multiple of it; 5.6 is just the average.

q: When beryllium was bombarded with alpha particles, it gave out a radiation that was not deflected by electric or magnetic fields and that knocked protons out of paraffin wax. Chadwick concluded that this radiation consists of:
o: Neutral particles with a mass about equal to that of a proton
x: No deflection means no charge; being able to knock out protons with high energy needs a particle of about the proton's mass. Gamma rays (no mass) could not do this, which was the earlier wrong idea; electrons and helium nuclei are charged and would be deflected.

q: Which ion has the same number of electrons as a neon atom (Z = 10) but more protons than electrons? (Z: N 7, O 8, F 9, Na 11)
x: All four ions have 10 electrons. Na⁺ has 11 protons (more than its electrons), while F⁻, O²⁻ and N³⁻ have 9, 8 and 7 protons, fewer than 10 electrons. Mixing up positive and negative ions gives the wrong choices.

q: The charge-to-mass ratio (e/m) of a proton is 9.58 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹. Taking the mass of an alpha particle as four times that of a proton, the e/m of an alpha particle is about:
x: An alpha particle (He²⁺) has twice the charge and four times the mass of a proton, so its e/m = (2/4) × 9.58 × 10⁷ = 4.79 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹. Forgetting the double charge gives one-quarter (2.40 × 10⁷).

q: The mass of a proton is approximately how many times the mass of an electron?
x: m(proton)/m(electron) = 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ / 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ ≈ 1836. The electron is the much lighter particle, so 1/1836 is the ratio the other way round.

q: According to Bohr's model, the angular momentum (mvr) of an electron in an allowed orbit is equal to:
x: Bohr's postulate: mvr = nh/2π, where n = 1, 2, 3 … so angular momentum is quantised in units of h/2π.

q: In Rutherford's experiment, a very few alpha particles bounced back from the thin gold foil at large angles. This showed that:
o: The positive charge and almost all the mass of the atom are packed into a tiny nucleus
Most of the atom is empty space
Electrons are spread evenly through the atom
The atom has no positive charge
x: Only a tiny, dense, positive centre could repel a heavy, fast alpha particle back. That most particles went straight through shows the atom is mostly empty space, which is a true conclusion but from a different observation.

q: Which electron transition in a hydrogen atom gives a line in the infrared region of the spectrum?
x: Lines ending at n = 3 form the Paschen series, in the infrared. Transitions ending at n = 2 (Balmer) are visible and those ending at n = 1 (Lyman) are ultraviolet; judging by the starting level instead of the final level is the slip.

q: Bohr's model of the atom could NOT explain:
o: The lines of the hydrogen spectrum
The stability of the hydrogen atom
The spectra of atoms with more than one electron
x: Bohr's model worked well for hydrogen (spectral lines, stability, ionisation energy) but failed for atoms with two or more electrons and for the fine splitting of lines.

q: Electrons in a sample of hydrogen atoms are excited to the n = 4 level. When they return to the ground state, the maximum number of different spectral lines that can be emitted is:
x: Possible jumps: 4→3, 4→2, 4→1, 3→2, 3→1 and 2→1, i.e. n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6. Counting only direct jumps from n = 4 gives 3.

q: For hydrogen, 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) with R = 1.10 × 10⁷ m⁻¹. The wavelength of the first (longest-wavelength) line of the Lyman series is about:
x: Lyman lines end at n₁ = 1; the first line is from n₂ = 2: 1/λ = R(1 − ¼) = ¾R, so λ = 4/(3 × 1.10 × 10⁷) = 1.21 × 10⁻⁷ m = 121 nm. 91 nm is the series limit (n₂ = ∞), and 655 nm is the first Balmer line.

q: What is the energy of one mole of photons of wavelength 300 nm? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
x: E = hc/λ = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.0 × 10⁸ / 3.0 × 10⁻⁷ = 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per photon; × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.97 × 10⁵ J ≈ 397 kJ mol⁻¹. A slip in converting nm to m shifts the answer by powers of ten.

q: The shape of an s orbital is:
x: An s orbital (l = 0) is spherically symmetrical about the nucleus. Dumbbell is the shape of a p orbital and double dumbbell describes most d orbitals.

q: The maximum number of electrons in an atom that can have n = 3 and l = 1 is:
x: n = 3, l = 1 is the 3p subshell, with m = −1, 0, +1 (three orbitals) holding 2 electrons each = 6. 18 is the capacity of the whole n = 3 shell and 10 is the 3d subshell.

q: The subshell with principal quantum number n = 4 and azimuthal quantum number l = 2 is:
x: l = 0, 1, 2, 3 correspond to s, p, d, f, so n = 4, l = 2 is 4d. Taking l = 2 as p (counting from 1) gives 4p.

q: How many electrons in an atom can have the quantum numbers n = 3 and m = 0?
x: For n = 3, l can be 0, 1 or 2; each has exactly one orbital with m = 0 (3s, one 3p, one 3d), so 3 orbitals × 2 electrons = 6. 3 counts orbitals instead of electrons, and 2 counts only the 3s orbital.

q: How many subshells are present in the shell with n = 3?
x: l takes values 0 to n − 1, i.e. 0, 1, 2 for n = 3: the 3s, 3p and 3d subshells. A 3f subshell would need l = 3, which is not allowed for n = 3; nine is the number of orbitals.

q: Which set of quantum numbers (n, l, m, s) describes an electron in a 3p orbital?
x: A 3p electron has n = 3 and l = 1, with m = −1, 0 or +1. The set with l = 2 is a 3d electron, l = 0 is 3s, and m = −2 is impossible when l = 1.

q: The maximum number of electrons that can occupy a subshell with azimuthal quantum number l = 3 is:
x: l = 3 (an f subshell) has 2l + 1 = 7 orbitals (m = −3 to +3), each holding 2 electrons, so 14. 7 counts orbitals only; 6 and 10 are the p and d capacities.

q: The ground-state electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24) is:
x: A half-filled 3d⁵ subshell with 4s¹ is more stable than 3d⁴ 4s², so chromium is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹, with six unpaired electrons. Filling strictly by the Aufbau order gives the tempting 3d⁴ 4s².

q: Which order of the subshells is in increasing energy, as used for filling by the Aufbau principle?
x: (n + l): 4s = 4, 3d = 5, 4p = 5, 5s = 5. 4s is lowest; among those with n + l = 5, the lower n fills first: 3d, then 4p, then 5s. Ordering by n alone puts 3d first.

q: How many unpaired electrons does a nitrogen atom (Z = 7) have in its ground state?
x: N is 1s² 2s² 2p³; by Hund's rule the three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins, so 3 unpaired electrons. Pairing two of them in one orbital gives 1.

q: Which arrangement breaks the Pauli exclusion principle?
o: Two electrons in the same 2s orbital, with opposite spins
Two electrons in the same 2s orbital, both with spin +½
One electron in each of the 2pₓ and 2pᵧ orbitals, with parallel spins
The 2s orbital filled before any 2p orbital
x: Two electrons in one orbital already share n, l and m, so they must differ in spin; both +½ gives identical sets of four quantum numbers. Parallel spins in different p orbitals follow Hund's rule and are allowed.

q: An atom X has the ground-state configuration [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴. The numbers of unpaired electrons in X and in the ion X²⁻ are:
x: 3p⁴: four electrons in three p orbitals, so one pair and two singles, giving 2 unpaired (Hund's rule). X²⁻ is 3p⁶, all paired, giving 0. Counting all four p electrons as unpaired gives 4.

q: A period 4 element has three unpaired electrons, all in its 4p subshell, in the ground state. Its atomic number and group are:
x: Three unpaired 4p electrons means 4p³: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p³, Z = 18 + 10 + 2 + 3 = 33 (arsenic), with 5 valence electrons, group VA. Counting only the p electrons gives group IIIA; 23 (vanadium) has its unpaired electrons in 3d, and 15 is phosphorus in period 3.
